summary.text: 火 is an indivisible picture of rising flames, used for ‘fire’. It has no internal sound or meaning component.

formation.text: Pictographic: the whole graph depicts flames rising. Its picture is the character; it is not a compound assembled from smaller components.

components.text: The whole character is a pictorial graph of rising flames, representing fire. It is not divided into smaller components; the character’s pronunciation does not make any part of it phonetic.

history.text: The curated examples show two distinct Shang oracle-bone forms. These images document graphic variation, not a proven sequence of changes. Warring States forms are described as more linear, with a stroke reversed and a horizontal added. The cited lexicon reports no bronze form in its own collection; this does not establish that none existed elsewhere.
A Han-period lexicographic account also describes flames rising and calls 火 pictographic. It is a later explanation, not independent proof of the graph’s Shang origin.

uncertainties.text: The cited oracle-bone examples establish Shang-period use, but the evidence does not date each inscription more precisely. The selected glyphs are modern vector renderings, not artifact photographs, and were not visually inspected for this entry.
The dossier does not settle competing Old Chinese reconstructions or proposed inherited comparisons; the Proto-Sino-Tibetan comparison is explicitly described as phonologically problematic.

senses.period: Shang-period oracle-bone use; individual inscription dates unresolved
senses.text: Oracle-bone examples include 火 in a literal fire context; the graph is analyzed as a picture of rising flames.

senses.period: Shang-period oracle-bone use; also attested in the Classic of Poetry
senses.text: 火 is attested as a name for the star 大火, identified with Antares. The evidence establishes this distinct use but not why the star bore the name.
‘Burn’ appears among the dossier’s dictionary glosses, but the evidence does not date this sense or establish its historical relation to ‘fire’.
‘Anger’ and ‘rage’ appear among the dossier’s dictionary glosses, but the evidence does not date these senses or establish their historical relation to ‘fire’.

limitations.text: The star-name is attested separately; no supported semantic path connects it to the literal fire sense.
The supplied gloss list does not establish chronology or development for ‘burn’ or ‘anger/rage’.

A proposed reading of 火 in one oracle-bone context as a phonetic loan for 禍 ‘calamity’ remains uncertain. The account attributes it to sound proximity and context but does not supply an independently checked sound comparison. If correct, the sign was reused for a different word thought to sound similar; this would be borrowing, not a change in the meaning ‘fire’.

overview.text: 火 is a whole-character picture of rising flames. The picture represents fire; there are no smaller sound or meaning parts to learn.

components.text: Read the whole graph as a picture of rising flames representing fire; it has no smaller component parts.
